item.title: Natural analogs for geoengineering suggest modest radiative plant gains
item.description: arXiv:2611.26845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) to limit global warming overshoot would reduce total solar radiation while increasing the proportion of diffuse light reaching Earth's surface, creating competing effects on plant growth. Analog studies using volcanic eruptions show impacts ranging from significantly negative to strongly positive, and numerical models suggest radiative effects from SAI would range from neutral to slightly positive. Here we show, using eddy covariance measurements at eight AmeriFlux sites (four maize and four forest), that radiative effects of smoke are positive across sites. This suggests that radiative effects from SAI would likely be modest but positive, consistent with numerical models. We attribute inconsistencies in the literature to limitations in the underlying assumptions and methods of previous analog studies; addressing these issues brings their results into agreement with our findings. More broadly, our results suggest that aerosols from wildfires, volcanoes, pollution, and SAI tend to moderately enhance photosynthesis.
item.dc:creator: Brendan Clark, Ben Kravitz, Daniele Visoni, Manuel Lerdau

item.title: Carbon dioxide responses shape estimates of Amazon forest vulnerability under solar geoengineering
item.description: arXiv:2611.26908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Amazon rainforest is vulnerable to warming and changes in rainfall, yet whether solar geoengineering can reduce conditions associated with forest loss remains uncertain. Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) can offset greenhouse-gas-driven warming without fully restoring regional hydroclimate. Here we assess Amazon forest vulnerability under mitigation, high-emission and SAI scenarios using a Carbon dioxide-dependent forest-sustainability threshold in a common climate phase space. By late century, SAI reduces projected Amazon warming from 5.49 degree Celsius under high emissions to 2.45 degree Celsius, but substantial drying and longer dry seasons persist. Under SAI, 44.7 percentage of analysed grid cells exceed the present-day threshold, compared with 8.7 percentage when the future Carbon dioxide-dependent threshold is considered. This contrast reveals that apparent forest protection depends strongly on the assumed resilience benefits of elevated Carbon dioxide. Our findings highlight the importance of hydroclimatic changes and Carbon dioxide-dependent vegetation responses in assessing the potential of solar geoengineering to reduce Amazon forest vulnerability.
item.dc:creator: Anupama K Xavier, Chris Jones

item.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
item.description: arXiv:2611.27641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.
item.dc:creator: Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, Christian Chwala

item.title: Stabilized negative viscosity governs ocean jets before, during and after they leave the coast
item.description: arXiv:2611.24399v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Eddies in rotating turbulence can feed the jets that spawn them, resulting in the negative viscosity phenomenon. Taken alone, a negative viscosity represents up-gradient eddy fluxes and is often referred to as "antifriction" or "antidiffusion". Mathematically, it leads to an ill-posed problem. In two-dimensional turbulence theory, this problem can be resolved by representing the transfer from small to large scales by a stabilized negative viscosity (SNV), in which a negative Laplacian viscosity is balanced by its positive biharmonic counterpart. In purely two-dimensional turbulence, by the Taylor identity, a negative viscosity is up-gradient transport of vorticity, which mixing cannot produce; on a slope, mixing of potential vorticity can mimic it, and we test for this. Using two years of wide-swath satellite altimetry (SWOT), we measure the eddy momentum flux across the five subtropical western boundary currents in each current's own frame. Along the continental slope the eddies act with a negative viscosity of order $-10^{3}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$, with the SNV structure resolved in the Gulf Stream and the Agulhas. At separation from the slope the sign reverses in all five currents, and the eddies brake the flow. Downstream, in the free jets, the negative viscosity returns on the cyclonic flank, strengthened to $-10^{4}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$. Separation is where the current leaves the strong topographic $\beta$ of the slope, the constraint that orders the eddy transfer. In an eddy-resolving reanalysis the SNV form holds across three ocean basins, with its shape parameter set by the deformation radius.
item.dc:creator: Boris Galperin, Alexei Chekhlov, Ilya Staroselsky, Semion Sukoriansky

item.title: Maximum updraft velocity beyond CAPE: the role of boundary layer dynamics and pressure perturbations
item.description: arXiv:2607.23627v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep convective updraft velocities influence precipitation extremes, lightning, and the planetary energy budget. Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) is widely used to explain maximum updraft velocity ($w_{\max}$), but updrafts are also influenced by entrainment, boundary layer dynamics, pressure perturbations, and condensate loading. However, the relative importance of these processes and how they interact to set $w_{\max}$ in individual clouds remains unclear. Here, we use neural networks validated across climate regimes to identify generalizable pre-storm predictors and in-cloud diagnostics of $w_{\max}$ in individual tracked clouds. We then distill these into compact, physically interpretable equations, using idealized radiative-convective equilibrium simulations spanning a range of sea surface temperatures and radiative cooling rates. For pre-storm prediction, CAPE and local mean boundary layer vertical velocity ($\overline{w_{bl}}$) together explain nearly half the variance in $w_{\max}$ across regimes ($R^2=0.47$). CAPE captures regime-mean differences, but it has little predictive value within a single simulation, where $\overline{w_{bl}}$ captures cloud-to-cloud variability, including low $w_{\max}$ at high CAPE. At the time of peak intensity, a simple approximate Bernoulli-like invariant combining maximum pressure perturbation and maximum cloud condensate explains 89% of the variance ($R^2=0.89$). The tight link between $w_{\max}$ and pressure perturbation is consistent with the sticky-thermal view and highlights dynamic pressure effects, often neglected in updraft theories. Both relationships remain skillful in additional simulations at horizontal grid spacings down to 125 m. These results highlight $\overline{w_{bl}}$ as an important regulator of convective intensity alongside CAPE, and indicate that dynamic pressure plays an important role within individual updrafts.
item.dc:creator: Bety Pechacova, Alejandro Casallas, Tom Beucler, Lokahith Agasthya, Caroline Muller
